units.t: Precise Words for Feelings.
Part one. Why the right word helps.
How are you feeling right now?
If you're like most people, the first answer that comes to mind is something like fine, good, tired or stressed.
Those words are useful, but they're a bit like describing every meal as food.
In this lesson, we'll look at why naming feelings more precisely can make a genuine difference, and then we'll collect some wonderfully exact words to do it with.
Let's start with the science.
In 2007, a team led by the psychologist Matthew Lieberman at the University of California, Los Angeles, put people into a brain scanner and showed them photos of faces.
The faces were angry, frightened or otherwise emotional.
Sometimes, people were asked to pick the word that described the emotion, such as angry or scared.
Other times, they did a different task with the same faces, like matching them by gender.
When people named the emotion, activity in the amygdala went down.
The amygdala is a small part of the brain that's heavily involved in detecting threats and raising the alarm.
At the same time, an area in the front of the brain, linked to managing emotions, became more active.
Lieberman's team called this affect labelling.
Putting a feeling into words seemed to take a little of the heat out of it.
The psychologist Lisa Feldman Barrett has taken this idea further.
She uses the term emotional granularity to describe how finely a person can tell their feelings apart.
Someone with low granularity might describe a whole range of bad days as just feeling awful.
Someone with high granularity might tell the difference between feeling disappointed, embarrassed, lonely and irritated.
It's like the difference between a map that only shows states and a map that shows every street.
Why would that matter?
Because different feelings call for different responses.
Disappointment might need a new plan.
Loneliness might need a phone call.
Irritation might just need a walk around the block.
If everything is just awful, it's much harder to know what to do.
There's some intriguing evidence behind this.
In a 2010 study, Todd Kashdan and his colleagues asked young adult social drinkers in the United States to record their emotions several times a day for three weeks.
On days when they felt intensely negative, people who were good at telling their negative feelings apart drank noticeably less than those who weren't.
Other studies have linked finer emotional distinctions with handling stress and setbacks better.
The research is still developing, and a bigger vocabulary isn't a magic cure for anything.
But the direction is encouraging.
The more precisely you can name what you feel, the more options you seem to have for dealing with it.
And one of the easiest ways to build that precision is to borrow some good words.
The cultural historian Tiffany Watt Smith, at Queen Mary University of London, made this the theme of a whole book.
Her Book of Human Emotions, published in 2015, gathers one hundred and fifty-four words from around the world for how we feel.
Some are ancient, some are modern, and some come from languages that name feelings English barely notices.
Her point is that emotions aren't fixed and universal in every detail.
The words a culture has can shape which feelings people notice, talk about and take seriously.
We won't get through a hundred and fifty-four today.
But here are some of the most useful.
Part two. Words borrowed from other languages.
English is famously good at borrowing, and some of our most precise feeling words come from elsewhere.
Our first is from German.
Schadenfreude.
S, C, H, A, D, E, N, F, R, E, U, D, E.
Here's an everyday example.
I felt a twinge of schadenfreude when the bloke who cut me off in traffic got pulled over a kilometre later.
Schadenfreude is pleasure at someone else's misfortune.
The German word is built from two parts.
Schaden means harm or damage, and Freude means joy.
So it's literally harm joy.
It's not a flattering feeling, which is probably why it's so useful to have a word for it.
It lets us admit to something we'd otherwise pretend we don't feel.
Researchers have studied it too.
In 2011, the psychologist Mina Cikara and her colleagues scanned the brains of dedicated baseball fans in the United States.
They were supporters of two fierce rivals, the Boston Red Sox and the New York Yankees.
When fans watched their rival team fail, even against a third team, areas of the brain linked to reward became more active.
The fans who showed the strongest response also said they'd be more likely to heckle, insult or even hit a rival fan.
If you've ever enjoyed your footy team's biggest rival losing a close one, you've felt it.
The useful thing about naming it is that it gives you a moment of distance.
Oh, that's schadenfreude.
Once it has a name, it's easier to notice, have a small private laugh at yourself, and move on.
Our second borrowed word is from French.
Ennui.
E, N, N, U, I.
It's pronounced on-wee.
For example, by the third week of the school holidays, a kind of ennui had settled over the whole house.
Ennui isn't the same as ordinary boredom.
Boredom is what you feel waiting in a queue at the post office.
It's short, and it has an obvious cause.
Ennui is deeper and heavier.
It's a restless, weary dissatisfaction, a sense that nothing much is interesting or worth the effort.
Here's a nice piece of history.
Ennui and the English word annoy come from the same Latin source.
Both go back to a phrase meaning something like, it is hateful to me.
French kept the weary, world-tired sense, while English took the irritated one.
Having the word ennui can help you spot a pattern.
If you're bored in a queue, you need the queue to move.
If you're feeling ennui, you might need something new in your life, a change of routine, a new challenge, or simply more rest.
And if a flat, heavy feeling hangs around for weeks, it's worth talking to your GP, or looking at the government's healthdirect website.
Our third borrowed word is from Portuguese.
Saudade.
S, A, U, D, A, D, E.
For example, going through my grandmother's recipe book, I felt a deep saudade for those Sunday lunches at her place.
Saudade is a longing for someone or something that's absent, and that may never come back.
It mixes love and sadness together.
It isn't only sad, because the love is part of the feeling.
It's often called untranslatable, and in a sense it is, because English needs a whole sentence to capture it.
Saudade runs all through Portuguese and Brazilian culture, especially the mournful Portuguese songs called fado.
In the 1600s, the Portuguese writer Francisco Manuel de Melo described it in a phrase that's often quoted.
Loosely translated, he called it a good that is suffered and an ill that is enjoyed.
That captures the strange sweetness of missing someone you loved.
Part three. Longing and mixed feelings.
Our next word is home-grown English.
Wistful.
W, I, S, T, F, U, L.
For example, she gave a wistful smile as the old family car was driven away by its new owner.
Wistful is a gentle, slightly sad longing.
It's softer than saudade.
It's the feeling of looking back at something with fondness and a small ache, without being truly upset.
Its origins are a little uncertain.
Dictionary makers think it probably grew from an old word, wistly, meaning intently or longingly, and was influenced by wishful.
Our next word is one with a long and colourful history.
Melancholy.
M, E, L, A, N, C, H, O, L, Y.
For example, there's a certain melancholy to a beach town in winter, when the kiosks are shut and the car parks are empty.
The word comes from Greek, and it literally means black bile.
Ancient Greek doctors believed the body contained four fluids, called humours, and that too much black bile made a person sad, thoughtful and withdrawn.
That theory has long been abandoned, but the word stayed.
In 1621, the English scholar Robert Burton published an enormous book called The Anatomy of Melancholy, and he kept adding to it for the rest of his life.
Today, melancholy usually means a quiet, reflective sadness, often with no single clear cause.
It's gentler than grief and more thoughtful than feeling down.
Many people find a little melancholy on a rainy Sunday almost pleasant, and plenty of the world's best-loved music lives in that mood.
Our next word is nostalgia.
N, O, S, T, A, L, G, I, A.
For example, hearing that song from year twelve on the radio filled me with nostalgia.
Nostalgia has a surprising history.
It was coined in 1688 by a Swiss medical student called Johannes Hofer.
He built it from two Greek words, nostos, meaning a return home, and algos, meaning pain.
Hofer described it as a disease.
He'd noticed it in Swiss soldiers fighting far from home, who became so homesick that they stopped eating and grew ill.
For a long time, nostalgia was treated as a medical problem.
Today, researchers see it very differently.
At the University of Southampton, psychologists including Constantine Sedikides and Tim Wildschut have spent years studying it.
They've found that nostalgia is usually a mixed but mostly positive feeling, and that it can make people feel more connected to others.
In one set of 2012 studies, led by Xinyue Zhou, people felt more nostalgic on colder days, and in colder rooms.
When they were asked to call up nostalgic memories, they judged the room to be warmer.
And in another experiment, people kept their hands in icy water for longer when they were thinking about nostalgic memories.
In a small way, nostalgia really does seem to warm us up.
Our final word is one that's often misused.
Ambivalent.
A, M, B, I, V, A, L, E, N, T.
For example, I'm ambivalent about the new job offer, because the money's better but I'd miss my team.
Many people use ambivalent to mean they don't care either way.
But that's closer to indifferent.
Ambivalent means you care a lot, in two directions at once.
The word was coined in German, around 1910, by the Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler.
It comes from Latin, ambi, meaning both, and valent, meaning being strong.
So ambivalence is two strong feelings pulling against each other.
It's a remarkably useful word for big life decisions.
Moving house, changing jobs, and even a child leaving home can all feel exciting and sad at the same time.
Knowing that this has a name, and that it's completely normal, can make it easier to sit with.
Here's a small exercise you can do right now, even if you're driving, because it only takes a moment of attention.
Notice how you're feeling at this moment.
Instead of fine or tired, try to find the most precise word you can.
Is it calm, restless, content, flat, a bit wistful, or quietly looking forward to something?
You don't need to change the feeling.
Just name it.
If you like, try it again at a few set moments in your day.
When you first sit down at work, when you walk in the door at home, or when you pull into the driveway.
Over a few weeks, you'll probably notice your inner vocabulary getting richer.
Fine starts to split into settled, relieved, a bit flat or quietly pleased.
And that small shift gives you more choices about what to do next.
To sum up, research suggests that naming feelings precisely can take some of the sting out of them and help you respond more wisely.
Words like schadenfreude, ennui, saudade, wistful, nostalgia and ambivalent give you sharper tools than just good or bad.
The more exact your words, the clearer your map of what's going on inside.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. In Matthew Lieberman's brain imaging study, what happened when people put a name to the emotion in a face?
Answer. Activity in the amygdala, a brain area involved in threat and alarm, went down.
Question two. What does the German word schadenfreude literally combine?
Answer. Harm and joy. Pleasure at someone else's misfortune.
Question three. Does ambivalent mean you don't care either way?
Answer. No. It means you have strong mixed feelings pulling in different directions.
That's the end of Precise Words for Feelings. Go gently. See you on the next one.
